lead: A polymer sample is not one molecule but many chains of different lengths. Its molar mass is therefore an average, and different experiments weight the chains differently. The number average counts every chain once; the weight average counts long chains more. Industry quotes molar mass and polydispersity to control processing, strength and solubility. The average you report must match the method you used: osmometry gives the number average, light scattering gives the weight average.
prereq: You need: 5.1 for degree of polymerization and 5.3 for how chains form.

sections.h3: Why a sample has an average

blocks.text: Chains start and stop at different moments during polymerization. A sample therefore contains a distribution: many short chains, many long chains, and a spread in between. Write N<sub>i</sub> for the number of chains whose molar mass is M<sub>i</sub> (M<sub>i</sub> in g/mol, N<sub>i</sub> a pure count). The index i runs over every chain length present.
M<sub>n</sub> = Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub> / Σ N<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: M<sub>n</sub> is the number-average molar mass in g/mol; N<sub>i</sub> is the number of chains of molar mass M<sub>i</sub>; the sum runs over all chain lengths.

blocks.text: This is the total mass divided by the total number of chains. Every chain counts once, whether it is short or long. Short chains are numerous but carry little mass, so they pull M<sub>n</sub> down.
M<sub>w</sub> = Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup> / Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub>
blocks.where: M<sub>w</sub> is the weight-average molar mass in g/mol; the extra M<sub>i</sub> in the numerator weights each chain by its mass.

blocks.text: This is the same as Σ w<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub>, where w<sub>i</sub> is the mass fraction of chains of molar mass M<sub>i</sub>. Long chains carry much mass, so M<sub>w</sub> rises above M<sub>n</sub>.

The ratio PDI = Mw / Mn is the polydispersity index. PDI = 1 means all chains are equal. A larger PDI means a broader distribution. The figure compares a narrow sample with a broad sample that has the same peak. How molar mass changes strength is in 5.5.
M<sub>n</sub> and M<sub>w</sub> are the two most quoted. Two more appear in polymer data sheets.

items: Viscosity-average molar mass M<sub>v</sub> comes from solution viscosity. It is defined by M<sub>v</sub> = (Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub><sup>1+a</sup> / Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub>)<sup>1/a</sup>, where a is the Mark-Houwink exponent. For flexible chains a is often about 0.5 to 0.8.
Z-average molar mass M<sub>z</sub> = Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub><sup>3</sup> / Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub><sup>2</sup>. It is very sensitive to the longest chains.

blocks.text: For a polydisperse sample, M<sub>n</sub> ≤ M<sub>v</sub> ≤ M<sub>w</sub> ≤ M<sub>z</sub>. The gaps grow as the distribution broadens. PDI = M<sub>w</sub> / M<sub>n</sub> is the usual measure of breadth.

M<sub>v</sub> is not a simple count average. The exponent a shifts the weighting toward the longer chains, which occupy more hydrodynamic volume and raise the viscosity more than short chains do. M<sub>z</sub> is used when the tail of very long chains matters, for example in GPC data analysis.
Each method weights chains by a different property, so each gives a particular average.

items: End-group analysis: titrate a known end group. If each chain has one titratable group, moles of group equal moles of chains. Divide sample mass by moles of chains to get M<sub>n</sub>. Works for low molar mass and known end groups.

Osmometry: measure osmotic pressure π of a dilute solution. The intercept of π/c against c gives RT/M<sub>n</sub>, where c is concentration in kg/m³, R is the gas constant 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, and T is kelvin. This gives M<sub>n</sub>; with c in kg/m³ the intercept gives M<sub>n</sub> in kg/mol, so multiply by 1000 to report it in g/mol.
Light scattering: scattered intensity grows with M<sub>w</sub>. A Zimm plot extrapolates to zero angle and zero concentration. This gives M<sub>w</sub>; full theory belongs to a physics course.
Viscometry: measure intrinsic viscosity [η] and use [η] = K M<sub>v</sub><sup>a</sup>. K and a are constants for a polymer-solvent pair at a temperature. This gives M<sub>v</sub>.
Gel permeation chromatography (GPC): molecules flow through porous beads. Small chains enter more pores and elute later. A detector records the full distribution, so all averages can be computed.

blocks.text: For routine quality control, GPC is the workhorse. For absolute M<sub>w</sub>, light scattering is used. For absolute M<sub>n</sub> at low mass, osmometry or end-group titration is used.

figure.caption: Two chain-length distributions scaled to the same peak height for comparison. The broad sample has long tails; those tails pull the weight average above the number average.

spec.aria: Two bell-shaped distributions of chain length; the broad one has the same peak but long tails on both sides, which pull the weight average above the number average.

examples.question: A polymer sample contains 10 g of chains with molar mass 10,000 g/mol and 30 g of chains with molar mass 40,000 g/mol. Find M<sub>n</sub>, M<sub>w</sub> and PDI.
steps: Moles of chains in first fraction = 10 g ÷ 10,000 g/mol = 0.0010 mol.
Moles in second fraction = 30 g ÷ 40,000 g/mol = 0.00075 mol.
Total moles = 0.0010 + 0.00075 = 0.00175 mol; total mass = 10 g + 30 g = 40 g.
examples.answer: M<sub>n</sub> ≈ 22,857 g/mol, M<sub>w</sub> = 32,500 g/mol and PDI ≈ 1.42.
examples.check:
mass1 = 10
M1 = 10000
mass2 = 30
M2 = 40000
n1 = mass1 / M1
n2 = mass2 / M2
total_moles = n1 + n2
total_mass = mass1 + mass2
mn = total_mass / total_moles
mw = (mass1 / total_mass) * M1 + (mass2 / total_mass) * M2
pdi = mw / mn
print(round(mn))
print(round(mw))
print(round(pdi, 2))

traps: Light scattering gives M<sub>w</sub>, not M<sub>n</sub>. Osmometry gives M<sub>n</sub>, not M<sub>w</sub>.
PDI = M<sub>w</sub> / M<sub>n</sub> is dimensionless. Convert both averages to the same unit (both g/mol or both kg/mol) before dividing; never mix them.
Do not average molar masses by simple arithmetic mean. Use the formula for the average the question names.
M<sub>v</sub> lies between M<sub>n</sub> and M<sub>w</sub>, not above M<sub>w</sub>, for normal polydisperse samples.
PDI near 1 means a narrow distribution, not necessarily a single chain length. PDI exactly 1 means all chains equal.

quiz.a: M<sub>n</sub> = Σ N<sub>i</sub> M<sub>i</sub> / Σ N<sub>i</sub>, where N<sub>i</sub> chains have molar mass M<sub>i</sub>. It is total mass divided by total number of chains.

quiz.q: Why is M<sub>w</sub> greater than M<sub>n</sub> for a polydisperse sample?
quiz.a: M<sub>w</sub> weights each chain by its mass, so long chains dominate. Short chains lower M<sub>n</sub> because they add many molecules but little mass.

quiz.q: A sample has 5 g of chains of 20,000 g/mol and 15 g of chains of 60,000 g/mol. Find M<sub>n</sub>.
Which method gives M<sub>n</sub>, which gives M<sub>w</sub>, and which gives M<sub>v</sub>? Use osmometry, light scattering, end-group analysis and viscometry.
quiz.a: Osmometry and end-group analysis give M<sub>n</sub>; light scattering gives M<sub>w</sub>; viscometry gives M<sub>v</sub>.

quiz.q: Write the Mark-Houwink relation and define its terms.
quiz.a: [η] = K M<sub>v</sub><sup>a</sup>; [η] is intrinsic viscosity, K and a are constants for a polymer-solvent-temperature system, and M<sub>v</sub> is viscosity-average molar mass.

quiz.q: PDI of a sample is 2.0 and M<sub>n</sub> = 25,000 g/mol. Find M<sub>w</sub>.
Why does GPC separate chains by length?
quiz.a: Porous beads let small chains enter more pores, so they take longer. Large chains pass through gaps and elute earlier, giving the distribution.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multi-detector GPC combines refractive index, light scattering and viscometry to get absolute averages without calibration. MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry gives the distribution of shorter chains. Molar mass control decides whether a resin can be injection moulded or spun into fibre, and it sets the toughness of polyethylene pipes. Search for 'gel permeation chromatography calibration', 'Mark-Houwink parameters' and 'Zimm plot'.
